source.title: Understanding Internal Representations of Recommendation Models with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Jia-Yin Wang; Xiaoyu Zhang; Wei-Zhi Ma; Zhi-Qiang Guo; Min Zhang

record.tranche_reason: Tests the predictive validity of explanations for learned SAE latents using a different method and model domain: explanations are used to predict activations on held-out recommendation cases.
record.gate_note: The relevant result is the held-out activation-prediction evaluation of explanations for RecSAE latents. These are SAE latents in recommendation models, not native neuron poles or language-model neurons. Other reported measures, including reconstruction performance and human relevance ratings, do not directly test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study builds RecSAE, a sparse-autoencoder probe for small recommendation models (64-dim user embeddings in BPRMF, LightGCN, SASRec and TiMiRec). It borrows OpenAI's explain-then-simulate scoring (N=5, Llama-3-8B) to report its own method's performance. Its units are SAE latents in recommenders, not native neurons in language models or InceptionV1. No result measures the neuron-pole shares, cross-model shares, canonical polysemantic neurons, neuron attribution graphs, or the explanation-fit gap that the versions name. The base-versus-RecSAE comparison in Table 4 compares the study's own method with a baseline. Its native-dimension counts concern a different kind of system, so they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that RecSAE extracts interpretable latents from varied recommendation models without altering them, and validates the derived concepts by predicting activations on new cases. Experts rate the concepts 3.89/4 for relevance. The method also enables targeted tuning. The 'above 0.6' statement refers only to the Amazon distribution in Figure 2.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Top-k sparse autoencoders to produce latent features in recommendation models, then has an LLM explain those features from item-activation sequences and tests the explanations on held-out recommendation cases; it does not audit native neuron poles.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported Amazon confidence distribution varies with the strength of the underlying recommendation model: the proportion of scores above 0.9 increases for stronger models.

fits_no_version.finding: Native dimensions of the 64-dim user representations, interpreted with the same explain-and-predict pipeline, rarely reach confidence ≥0.8. For example, 5 of 64 for Amazon BPRMF (LLM) and 10 of 64 for SASRec. RecSAE latents reach far more, e.g. 110 to 193 of about 1,000 on Amazon (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small recommendation models, few native embedding dimensions receive high-confidence simulated explanations; SAE latents receive more.

fits_no_version.finding: The confidence distribution of RecSAE latents on Amazon shifts upward for stronger base recommenders (Figure 2, Section 5.2.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpretability scores of SAE latents in recommenders rise with base-model recommendation accuracy.

record.problems: The text gives no exact confidence-distribution values for the plotted models. Verification uses N=5 activated construction examples per latent and a small held-out sample; the paper does not report uncertainty intervals for the confidence results. The tested units and models differ from those in the neuron-pole claims.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported result directly measures a version in the claim. Reconstruction metrics, human relevance ratings, and targeted-tuning results concern RecSAE's recommendation-specific framework rather than the stated neuron-pole claims.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or one-job, two-job or unexplained shares.
No language models, dense or MoE, and no scale comparison.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron analysis.
No neuron-level architecture or regularization comparison and no vision models. SAE-versus-base gains concern latents, not native neurons.
No attribution graphs or circuit analysis.
No comparison of explanations judged on activating examples against prediction of where native neurons fire.
No simulation scoring of language-model neuron explanations on new text and no explainer-strength comparison. Only Llama-3-8B is used.

missing.what: Base (native-dimension) versus RecSAE counts of concepts with P≥0.8, by model and dataset, under TF-IDF and LLM pipelines. This bears on V7 or V4 only by analogy, for non-language recommender models.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 link and its limits_scope label are removed. The study evaluates its own SAE latents in 64-dim recommender embeddings, which is a different unit and system kind from the claim's language-model and vision neurons. The pipeline copies the OpenAI scoring setup (an original source for V7) only as a tool.

versions.untested_parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or their one-job, two-job, or unexplained shares.
No comparison of neuron-pole shares across language models, model sizes, or dense and mixture-of-experts architectures.
No analysis of InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
No comparison of architecture, regularization, or tools as explanations of neuron interpretability rates, and no InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
No attribution-graph test of whether a large model's own neurons suffice as circuit units.
Tests held-out activation prediction for explanations of RecSAE latents in recommendation models, not native language-model neurons or explanations evaluated on new text.
Does not evaluate native neuron explanations on new text or compare stronger explainer models as described.

rows.subject: BPRMF, LightGCN, and SASRec (Amazon dataset; aggregate description)
rows.operation_detail: Used LLM-generated latent concepts to predict activation levels on held-out activated and non-activated cases; reported the confidence-score distribution.

conditions.value: new cases; positive and non-activated cases

rows.measure: Concept confidence score, defined as accuracy in classifying held-out cases using predicted activation levels; the text describes the distribution but gives no exact fractions.
rows.value: The majority of latents have confidence scores above 0.6; as the base recommendation model becomes stronger, the proportion above 0.9 increases.
rows.note: The text gives an aggregate description of the Amazon distributions across the three plotted models, not model-specific numerical values. RecSAE latents are not native neurons.
rows.check: The subject is RecSAE latents in recommendation models, not native neurons in language models. The confidence score is the study's own method performance on 10 held-out cases per latent (5 activated, 5 non-activated). V6 concerns explanations of native neurons that fit activating examples but fail to predict firing. This row shows no such gap and has no comparison of inspection-based versus prediction-based judgement. The value is only a verbal description of Figure 2 (majority above 0.6), so a state against any version cannot be read.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Amazon dataset; plotted BPRMF, LightGCN, and SASRec models
reader_labels.reason: Held-out prediction scores are described as above 0.6 for a majority of latents, and the proportion above 0.9 varies with base-model strength; this indicates some predictive validity and model-dependent variation rather than a uniformly low score (r1).
